transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-03
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Helix CTO), Evan Chen (Helix Platform Engineer), Liam O'Neill (Helix Security)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery on private deployment. Discussed VPC peering, private endpoints, region constraints, KMS/HSM, audit logs, and next steps for pilot + security docs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining - Jordan from Redwood. Priya and I are on from the team. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Marta Ruiz: Hi, Jordan, yeah thanks. I'm Marta, CTO at Helix. Evan and Liam on the line as well.
[00:12] Evan Chen: Hey all.
[00:13] Liam O'Neill: Hi.
[00:15] Jordan Lee: Great. Goal for today is to understand your networking constraints and whether Private/VPC deployment fits - also region/residency needs, and any compliance gating. We'll talk options: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, but focus on Private/VPC.
[00:30] Marta Ruiz: Right, we're evaluating Redwood because we need inference inside our VPC for PHI-like data. We want no traffic going over public internet and need control over keys - ideally our KMS. Also, some regs require data to remain in eu-west-1 or us-east-1 depending on the product.
[00:45] Priya Kapoor: Totally. Quick Q: is the priority pure data residency, or also egress controls and network isolation for compliance?
[00:50] Marta Ruiz: All of the above. Data residency for certain workloads, egress restrictions, and we need audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[00:58] Evan Chen: And we have existing peering across multiple accounts in our org, so we want to know if Redwood supports VPC peering, or if we must use private endpoints, transit gateway, etc. Latency is another consideration for real-time features.
[01:12] Jordan Lee: Understood. High level: Redwood Private offers a customer-managed VPC connection model - you can either peer with our subnet, set up PrivateLink-style endpoints, or use a transit gateway. Each has tradeoffs. Peering is simple but limited by routing and overlapping CIDRs; Private Endpoints give stronger control and don't require route table changes but require our private endpoint infrastructure. Transit gateway works at scale.
[01:40] Liam O'Neill: For KMS: can we use our key store (AWS KMS or on-prem HSM)? We can't allow Redwood to manage plaintext keys for the sensitive workloads.
[01:50] Priya Kapoor: Yes, for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS via key policies and envelope encryption. We support customer-managed CMKs in AWS KMS and there are HSM integration options for on-prem. For hosted we offer BYOK for enterprise, but dedicated/private gives tighter control.
[02:06] Marta Ruiz: Ok good. How does the network egress look - do we still need NAT?
[02:11] Jordan Lee: If you fully peer and route, traffic to Redwood endpoints stays internal; egress to third-party services from our side depends on the setup. We can publish a list of outbound IPs for any required firewall whitelisting. For PrivateLink endpoints, you call a private endpoint inside your VPC and traffic doesn't traverse the public internet.
[02:30] Evan Chen: What's the recommended approach when you have multiple accounts and region constraints? We currently have workloads in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 and cannot move certain datasets across regions.
[02:40] Priya Kapoor: We typically recommend colocating inference capacity in the region where the sensitive data lives. For multi-region, you can set up region-specific private deployments or dedicated pools per region and route requests by policy. There is a cost tradeoff for multi-region dedicated capacity.
[03:00] Jordan Lee: Also, if latency is critical, we can run a small dedicated pool in-region and use cross-region fallback only for non-sensitive workloads.
[03:12] Marta Ruiz: Makes sense. For our compliance, we need full audit logs and SAML SSO. Does Redwood support pushing logs to our SIEM?
[03:20] Priya Kapoor: Yes - audit logs and request-level metadata can be exported to your logging endpoint or S3. We can also integrate with SIEMs via syslog or forwarding connectors. SSO via SAML is supported for the control plane.
[03:33] Liam O'Neill: How about network ACLs and security groups - do we manage those? We want explicit deny-by-default and to limit egress ports.
[03:41] Jordan Lee: You retain control of your VPC security groups and NACLs. Redwood will provide recommended security group rules and required ports/IP ranges. For private endpoints we provide the endpoint network configuration.
[03:55] Evan Chen: Can you walk through a simple peering setup? We're worried about overlapping CIDRs.
[04:00] Priya Kapoor: Sure. Typical approach: if CIDRs overlap, peering isn't possible - then you either use PrivateLink or a transit gateway with NAT and route translation, or re-IP. For peering: create a VPC peering connection to our ingress VPC, update route tables for the specific subnets, and open security groups. We'll provide the exact subnets and prefixes we expose.
[04:28] Marta Ruiz: What about IP whitelisting? Do you have a fixed set of addresses?
[04:32] Jordan Lee: For dedicated/private we provide a set of internal prefixes and also publish static egress IPs if needed for outbound whitelisting. For hosted public API those IPs change, but for private deployments they're stable.
[04:45] Evan Chen: Great. On latency: we need p95 < 200ms for short prompts. How realistic is that inside a private peering setup?
[04:53] Priya Kapoor: That depends on model size, batching, and hardware profile. For a medium sized model on dedicated GPUs colocated in us-east-1, p95 under 200ms for small prompts is achievable. We'll need to run benchmarks with your prompt set. That's why the pilot is useful.
[05:10] Jordan Lee: We'll propose a pilot with a small dedicated pool in us-east-1 - run your typical workload and measure latency/cost and verify network configuration.
[05:20] Marta Ruiz: Sounds good. A few non-network questions: Do you have SOC 2 Type II and ISO certifications?
[05:26] Priya Kapoor: Redwood has SOC 2 Type II and is working toward ISO; we can send the attestation and our security whitepaper. For Private deployments we also offer additional contractual clauses.
[05:36] Liam O'Neill: Encryption in transit and at rest?
[05:39] Jordan Lee: TLS in transit and default encryption at rest. For key control you can use your CMKs for envelope encryption.
[05:44] Evan Chen: If we do PrivateLink, is there any change to how we authenticate requests? We want mTLS.
[05:50] Priya Kapoor: We support mTLS and token-based authentication. For private endpoints we can enforce mTLS, and you can layer additional SAML or OIDC-based controls at the control plane.
[05:59] Marta Ruiz: Okay. Can you share the network diagram and a connectivity checklist?
[06:03] Jordan Lee: We'll send a diagram and a checklist - include required ports, subnets, IP ranges, and steps for peering or PrivateLink.
[06:10] Evan Chen: Do you have any documentation on transit gateway setups? We use TGW internally for cross-account routing.
[06:16] Priya Kapoor: Yes, we have a TGW integration guide. We'll include that. Also note: TGW can simplify multi-account setups but requires additional configuration and sometimes an AWS account that hosts the TGW.
[06:28] Marta Ruiz: For cost - can you summarize differences between Dedicated and Private in terms of pricing?
[06:33] Jordan Lee: Briefly: Dedicated reserved capacity is capacity we allocate to you - priced on a monthly commit (and discounts for annual). Private VPC deployment includes a control-plane fee plus the dedicated/generally reserved compute. Hosted is pay-as-you-go. We'll follow up with a pricing band for the pilot.
[06:50] Evan Chen: Any constraints around region availability - e.g., eu-west-1 vs eu-central-1?
[06:55] Priya Kapoor: We support common commercial regions. Some specialized regions (gov, secret) require separate agreements. For EU we typically support eu-west-1 and eu-central-1; availability depends on capacity and GPU type. We'll confirm region availability for the model/hardware you need.
[07:12] Liam O'Neill: For audit logs forwarding, do you support pushing to our S3 with SSE-KMS using our key?
[07:18] Priya Kapoor: Yes, we can forward logs to your S3 with SSE-KMS and you can control the CMK. We can also stream to your SIEM via secure forwarders.
[07:26] Marta Ruiz: Good. One more: data retention policy - can we control how long requests are retained on Redwood side?
[07:33] Jordan Lee: Yes - for Private deployments you can set retention policies and disable retention for certain workloads. We'll include details in the security docs.
[07:42] Evan Chen: Are there limitations on model sizes or quantization for Private? We may want to run larger models and use int8 quantization.
[07:50] Priya Kapoor: The runtime supports several quantization profiles and model sizes. For very large models you may need additional GPU types and kernel support - we'll validate model compatibility as part of onboarding.
[08:02] Marta Ruiz: Ok, that helps. Let's talk timeline: We want to kick a pilot in the next two weeks if possible.
[08:09] Jordan Lee: We can aim for pilot kickoff week of 2026-11-16. Steps: share network diagram + checklist, Helix confirms regions and compliance docs, Redwood provides SOW and pilot pricing, then environment prep and connectivity tests.
[08:22] Evan Chen: On connectivity test: do you provide a test harness or iperf-like tool?
[08:26] Priya Kapoor: We'll provide a connectivity checklist with endpoints and a small test harness for latency/throughput probes and simple inference calls to validate end-to-end.
[08:35] Liam O'Neill: For the contract side, we need standard security addenda and data processing agreements.
[08:41] Jordan Lee: We'll include DPAs and standard security addenda. If you need additional clauses we can surface them to legal.
[08:47] Marta Ruiz: Great. Any concerns with IP ranges changing mid-pilot?
[08:52] Jordan Lee: For private deployments we commit to stable internal prefixes for the pilot period. If anything changes we'll notify in advance and coordinate maintenance windows.
[08:59] Evan Chen: Cool. A few clarifications: will Redwood be able to access logs in plaintext? We want strict role separation.
[09:05] Priya Kapoor: Access policies can be configured. For sensitive workloads you can restrict Redwood access and require that logs be forwarded into your own S3 and not retained on our side. We can set role-based controls and enforce separation.
[09:18] Marta Ruiz: Excellent. That addresses most of our questions.
[09:22] Jordan Lee: Quick recap and next steps: we'll send the network diagram + TGW guide + connectivity checklist + SOC2 attestation + draft SOW and pilot pricing. Priya will follow up with IP ranges and test harness. Helix will confirm regions and security docs.
[09:35] Evan Chen: Sounds good.
[09:36] Liam O'Neill: Thanks everyone.
[09:38] Jordan Lee: Thanks folks - we'll follow up via email.

End of transcript.
